expectations.evidence: Beyond the 'Related documents' list at the top, a dedicated 'Evidence and open questions' section immediately follows it, giving inline provenance for each fact (source, who reported it, and its confidence level) rather than leaving provenance implicit in a document list.

expectations.text: The document states explicitly that the items the user listed are design choices rather than requirements
expectations.evidence: Context section: 'None of these is a requirement in the architectural sense — a requirement is a constraint on the *problem*... not a prescription of the *solution*.' And: 'This document treats those five items as candidate solutions to evaluate, not as given constraints — each is carried into the Design and Tradeoff analysis sections and judged against the requirements below, exactly like any other alternative.'

expectations.text: None of the saga pattern, microservices, Redis caching, gRPC or feature flags appears in the requirements section as a requirement
expectations.evidence: The Requirements section (FR1-FR4, NFR1-NFR4, lines 59-98) contains only problem-level statements (explicit steps, failure attribution, no stranded side effects, automatic recovery, 100% attribution, reduced defect rate, incremental/reversible delivery, no consistency regression). None of the five named technologies is used as a requirement; they are explicitly deferred to the Design and Tradeoff sections instead.

expectations.text: At least one requirement is derived from the 2% checkout failure rate, with a target and a goal
expectations.evidence: NFR2 is the requirement derived from the 2% figure ('Reduced defect-driven failure rate. The share of the ~2% failure rate attributable to system defects... should drop measurably after this refactor ships.') but the document explicitly withholds a target: 'No numeric target is set here because the cause breakdown of the current 2% is not available... Setting a target... before that breakdown exists would be a number nobody has verified.' A goal is present; a target is explicitly and deliberately absent, so the assertion's two-part bar (target AND goal) is not met by any requirement tied to the 2% figure.

expectations.text: At least one requirement is derived from the inability to identify which checkout step failed, expressed measurably
expectations.evidence: NFR1 — '100% attribution. Of checkout attempts that fail, 100% must be attributable to a specific step, within the existing observability toolchain, without a code change or ad hoc log-grepping. Today this is effectively 0%...' This gives both a measurable target (100%, vs. today's 0%) and is explicitly derived from the attribution problem.

expectations.text: The user's proposed technologies appear in the design or the tradeoff analysis, each tied to the requirement it would serve
expectations.evidence: Design section maps each technology to a dimension tied to specific requirements: Dimension 1 ties the saga pattern to FR2/FR3/FR4; Dimension 2 ties microservices splitting to independent-scaling/ownership drivers (evaluated against the same FRs/NFRs); Dimension 3 ties gRPC to FR2/NFR1 ('Evaluated against FR2... and NFR1'); Dimension 4 ties Redis to the FR3 idempotency/state-store need; Dimension 5 ties feature flags to NFR3. Each also reappears as a labeled row in the Tradeoff table (e.g., '[Dim 3 — protocol, only if split] gRPC between services, as requested').

expectations.text: At least one of the user's proposed technologies is questioned, deferred, or shown not to be needed for the stated problem
expectations.evidence: The decision explicitly defers three of the five: 'do **not** commit to a physical microservices split, gRPC, or Redis as part of this phase.' Redis is additionally shown not needed for its most literal reading: the 'Redis as a general checkout-time read cache' row states 'Not connected to FR2/FR3/FR4 (attribution/reliability) at all — solves a latency problem that was never stated as a requirement here.'

expectations.text: Where information is missing, the document either labels an assumption or asks a focused question with a recommended answer
expectations.evidence: The 'Assumptions and open questions' section lists five explicit assumptions (e.g., 'Current checkout architecture is unknown... This document assumes checkout exists today as some form of single deployable...'), each with its implication stated. The Related documents section also lists what's missing and flags that 'several items below are stated as explicit assumptions rather than verified facts.'

expectations.text: Every requirement in the document carries a goal and a stated way to prove it is met
expectations.evidence: Only NFR1 states an explicit verification method: 'Target should be validated by deliberately failing each step in a staging environment and confirming attribution works, not just estimated.' The other seven requirements state a goal but no verification method: FR1 ('Checkout must be modeled as an ordered sequence of named, individually observable steps') has no stated way to confirm it's met; FR3 ('Every side-effecting step must have a defined compensating action') has no stated proof procedure; FR4, NFR2, NFR3, and NFR4 likewise state only the goal/constraint with no accompanying verification method. The assertion requires this for 'every requirement,' and 7 of 8 lack it.

expectations.text: The document questions the premise that a language rewrite is the right axis of decision, rather than accepting Rust-versus-Go as given
expectations.evidence: Section 'A framing risk this RFC flags before going further' states: 'A rewrite in a faster language only fixes the problem if the 12 seconds is actually dominated by CPU-bound PDF rendering ... rather than by I/O.' And: 'If A1 is false ... neither Rust nor Go will meaningfully help, and the right fix is pipeline/query optimization or parallel fetching, not a language rewrite.' This is carried through: the launch strategy makes a profiling spike step 1 'before writing Go code,' and the decision section calls this 'the single largest risk to the value of this entire effort.' This is substantive engagement, not a token caveat -- it genuinely contests whether the language axis matters at all pending root-cause data.

expectations.text: Notes that the 12-second figure has not been attributed to a root cause, and names what would attribute it (a profile, a benchmark, or a breakdown by stage)
expectations.evidence: 'No profiling data for the current service was available to this RFC's author, so this is stated as an assumption, not a verified fact.' Open verification item 1: 'Profile the current Python service on the 40-page case to confirm Assumption A1 (CPU-bound rendering vs. I/O-bound data fetch).' The dynamic diagram section also says: 'instrumenting the boundary between them [data assembly vs. render] ... is the cheapest way to de-risk this whole RFC' -- naming a stage breakdown explicitly.

expectations.text: The tradeoff analysis includes at least one alternative that is not a rewrite in Rust or Go
expectations.evidence: The 'Alternatives analysis (Tradeoff)' section opens with: 'Only one dimension is actually open in this RFC -- the implementation language -- since the rewrite itself and the general architecture above are treated as given by the request.' The tradeoff table has exactly two rows: 'Go' and 'Rust'. The document explicitly relegates the non-rewrite option to 'Out of scope': 'Whether to rewrite at all vs. optimize the existing Python service (the request already decided on a rewrite; this RFC only picks the language).' No third alternative (e.g., optimizing/parallelizing the existing Python service, swapping to a different PDF library, offloading the hot path via a native extension, using an off-the-shelf renderer) is ever analysed with pros/cons/risk in the tradeoff section itself.

expectations.text: Both alternatives the user named are still analysed fairly, with pros, cons and risks
expectations.evidence: The table gives Go pros (compiled speedup, mature invoice-shaped PDF libraries, simple concurrency, fast iteration, possible ecosystem fit) and cons (GC pauses, less feature-complete PDF ecosystem for advanced typography) plus two risk rows. Rust gets symmetric treatment: pros (no GC, predictable tail latency, memory safety) and cons (smaller/less mature PDF ecosystem, steeper learning curve, no confirmed in-house experience) plus two risk rows. Neither side is analysed as a strawman; the write-up gives each a real edge case.

expectations.text: The performance requirement is stated as a target with a unit and a measurement method, and is tied to what the finance team needs rather than to a language
expectations.evidence: Non-functional requirements: 'This RFC proposes p95 <= 2s for a 40-page invoice as a working target -- this number is not validated against finance's actual tolerance and should be confirmed with them before being treated as an SLO.' Unit (seconds) and measurement method (p95 percentile) are both present, and the target is framed around the finance-facing case, not any language's benchmark. Caveat noted in eval_feedback below: the actual number is invented/unconfirmed rather than derived from a real finance input.

expectations.text: Every risk in the tradeoff analysis carries impact, probability, mitigation and contingency
expectations.evidence: All four risk rows in the table are fully populated: 'GC pause spikes tail latency...' (Impact: Medium, Probability: Low-Medium, Mitigation: 'Tune GOGC / use a pooled-object pattern...', Contingency: 'Fall back to bounded worker-pool concurrency...'); the Go PDF-ecosystem gap risk (Medium/Medium, with diff-testing mitigation and patch/secondary-renderer contingency); the Rust learning-curve risk (High/High, with spike+pairing mitigation and 'fall back to Go mid-project' contingency); and the Rust PDF-library-gap risk (Medium/Medium, with a spike-evaluation mitigation and a wrap-a-mature-renderer contingency). No risk row is missing any of the four fields.

expectations.text: Reaches an explicit decision rather than only listing options
expectations.evidence: '## The decision \n\n**Decision: rewrite the PDF generation service in Go.**' followed by reasoning tied to each requirement -- an unambiguous single-language recommendation, not a menu of options.

expectations.text: Says plainly, in the document or in the reply, that the framing was challenged and why
expectations.evidence: reply.md: 'Since you said "pick one," I picked -- but a few things in your framing don't hold up as given, and I want to be upfront about them rather than bury the caveats,' followed by: 'I don't know whether that 12 seconds is actually CPU-bound rendering, or if it's dominated by data fetching ... if the bottleneck is I/O, rewriting in either Rust or Go won't fix it -- you'd be solving the wrong problem.' This states plainly, in the reply, that the framing was challenged and why.
